items.stem: In this book, what does mind refer to?

options.text: The capacities a system has for taking in information, holding it in usable form, and using it to guide what it does.
options.why: Correct. Perceiving, remembering, reasoning and deciding are all ways of turning information into something useful, and together they are what the book means by a mind.

options.text: The felt, qualitative character of a system's experiences, such as what it is like to see red.
options.why: That is qualia, which the chapter names and then deliberately sets aside as one part of the mind rather than the whole of it.

options.text: The subset of a system's processing that the system can report on and is aware of doing.
options.why: This is closer to one everyday sense of consciousness. The book's definition covers a great deal that a system need not be aware of doing.

options.text: Whatever a system does that could not be predicted from a complete description of its physical parts.
options.why: Nothing in the definition requires unpredictability, and defining a mind this way would build a substantive philosophical claim into what is meant to be a neutral starting point.

items.stem: In class we noted that a Venus flytrap does not snap shut on the first touch of its trigger hairs, but on the second, provided the second comes soon enough. Why was that case raised?

options.text: It satisfies the working definition in something with no neurons at all.
options.why: Correct. The point of the example is the discomfort it causes: the definition is met by a plant, which shows that the definition has no crisp boundary to check a system against.

options.text: It shows that holding information over time requires neurons, which is what separates minds from plants.
options.why: The example shows the opposite. The plant holds a count over an interval without any neurons, which is exactly why it is awkward for a tidy boundary.

options.text: It is a counterexample to the definition, demonstrating that the definition needs a further condition added to it.
options.why: The chapter and the lecture both decline to add that condition. The definition is offered as a starting place rather than a test, and where the line falls is a live debate.

options.text: It illustrates that behavior which looks like counting is usually a reflex that only resembles information processing.
options.why: The lecture does not dismiss it that way. It treats the flytrap as genuinely holding a count, which is what makes the case interesting rather than easy.

items.stem: How does the chapter distinguish qualia from consciousness?

options.text: Consciousness is used broadly; qualia name something narrower, the raw feel of an experience.
options.why: Correct. The two are closely tied and are not simply the same thing, which is why the chapter introduces both rather than treating one as a synonym for the other.

options.text: Qualia are a property of human minds, whereas consciousness is attributed to any system that processes information.
options.why: Neither term is restricted by species in the chapter, and the broad information-processing definition is of mind, not of consciousness.

options.text: Consciousness is the felt character of experience; qualia are the mechanisms in the brain that produce it.
options.why: This reverses the two and adds a mechanistic claim the chapter does not make. Qualia are the felt character itself, not what produces it.

options.text: Qualia can be studied experimentally, whereas consciousness is set aside as beyond the reach of science.
options.why: The chapter sets the whole cluster aside as hard and distinctive, and it does not sort the two by how tractable they are.

items.stem: What is the mind–body problem?

options.text: The question of how the mind relates to the physical stuff it seems to arise from.
options.why: Correct. The book often puts it as the relation between mind and the physical rather than the brain specifically, because whether a brain is required is part of what is in question.

options.text: The problem of explaining how the brain coordinates the many organs of the body at once.
options.why: This is a question in physiology. The mind–body problem is about the relation between mental and physical description, not about bodily coordination.

options.text: The difficulty of measuring mental states given that only behavior can be observed directly.
options.why: This is closer to the methodological worry behaviorism raised. The mind–body problem is asked even where measurement is not at issue.

options.text: The question of which mental capacities a system must have before it counts as having a mind at all.
options.why: That is the boundary question the working definition leaves open. It is a separate issue from how mind relates to the physical.

items.stem: A student concludes that because this chapter's questions cannot be settled by experiment, the positions in it are matters of opinion and one is as good as another. Where does that go wrong?

options.text: They are decided by consistency, by fit with what else is known, and by explaining most while assuming least.
options.why: Correct. The chapter is explicit that different deciding tools are not the absence of a fact of the matter, and that judged by those tools the answers are not equal.

options.text: It is wrong because the positions can in fact be tested experimentally once the right measurements are designed.
options.why: The chapter denies this. Some of these questions are prior to measurement, because they are questions about which measurements would count.

options.text: It is wrong because most scientists have converged on one position, which settles the matter.
options.why: Convergence is reported, but the chapter treats it as the result of argument rather than as what makes the position correct, and it notes the disagreement stays live.

options.text: It is right about the reasoning but wrong about the conclusion, since philosophy aims at clarity rather than at truth.
options.why: The chapter does not restrict philosophy to clarifying. It has philosophy evaluating whether a set of commitments hangs together, which is aimed at getting the answer right.

items.stem: The chapter sets consciousness aside for most of the course. Explain what makes that move legitimate, and name the view that resists the separation it depends on.
items.answer: Consciousness can be pried apart from the rest of the mind at least descriptively: a system might perceive, remember and reason at a high level, and whether anything is experienced along the way stays a separate question. Because the rest of mental life can be studied without settling that question, setting it aside costs the chapter little while keeping it honest about what has been postponed. The move would not be legitimate on a view that holds mind simply is consciousness, since on that view nothing would be left to study once consciousness was set aside.
rubric: States that consciousness can be separated from the rest of the mind at least descriptively.
Gives the reason: a system could perceive, remember or reason while whether anything is experienced stays open.
Notes that setting it aside is a decision about scope, not a claim that it is unreal or unimportant.
Identifies the view that mind simply is consciousness as the one that resists the separation.

items.stem: The module opens with two questions: how mind relates to brain, and what it would take for something other than a human brain to have a mind. What is the chapter's claim about their relationship?

options.text: They are one question asked twice, the second being the first asked about a different kind of stuff.
options.why: Correct, and it is the move the whole module turns on. Whatever we conclude about how minds relate to brains simultaneously constrains what else could have a mind, so the two cannot be settled separately.

options.text: They are separate questions, and nothing about the first settles anything about the second.
options.why: The chapter does not hold the machine question back. It treats an answer to either as constraining the other, which is why machine cases appear throughout rather than at the end.

options.text: The first is a scientific question and the second a matter of definition, so they are answered by different methods.
options.why: Both are treated as substantive, and neither is settled by stipulating a meaning. The chapter is explicit that fixing what "mind" means is only a starting place.

options.text: The second is a special case of the first, applying only once a machine is sophisticated enough to be a candidate.
options.why: Nothing waits on sophistication. The question is what kind of thing could have a mind at all, and it is asked of a thermostat as readily as of a chatbot.

items.stem: The chapter describes a single moment of fear twice — once as amygdala, adrenaline and a pounding heart, once as the lurch and the wish for it to stop. What problem is that pair of descriptions used to introduce?

options.text: Whether they are two accounts of one event, or one event rendered in two languages.
options.why: Correct. Both descriptions are of the very same instant, and what their relationship is turns out to be the mind–body problem in miniature.

options.text: Whether the physical description is complete, or leaves out a causal step.
options.why: The physical description is presented as leaving out no physical event. The puzzle is not a gap in it, but what the second description adds.

options.text: Whether fear is a genuine emotion or a reflex that only resembles one.
options.why: The chapter does not question that the fear is real. It questions how the felt account relates to the physical one.

options.text: Whether the felt description could be checked by anyone other than the person having it.
options.why: This is a question about evidence — whether a felt report can be checked from outside. Here the issue is what the two descriptions are descriptions of, which is prior to it.

items.stem: Why does a course about how minds evolved open with a chapter of philosophy rather than biology?

options.text: Because treating the mind as a natural object with a history assumes both that there is a mind to have one and that science can reach it.
options.why: Correct. Both assumptions have been doubted by serious people, and clearing that ground is what makes "the evolution of the mind" a coherent subject rather than a figure of speech.

options.text: Because the philosophical questions are the ones students find most engaging, so they make a good opening.
options.why: The chapter gives no such reason. It argues the questions are load-bearing for everything after them, not that they are the most interesting.

options.text: Because the biology cannot be understood without first knowing the named positions on the mind–body problem.
options.why: §1.2.6 says the opposite about the positions: they are scaffolding, and not what a student should carry forward.

options.text: Because philosophy and science answer the same questions by different methods, so either could come first.
options.why: The chapter distinguishes them sharply. Some questions must be settled before hypothesis-testing can begin, which is an order, not a choice.

items.stem: The chapter says no measurement can settle what "mind" means or what would count as a physical explanation of one. What reason does it give?

options.text: Because these are questions about which measurements would count in the first place.
options.why: Correct, and it is a sharper claim than "we lack the instruments." A measurement cannot settle a question whose answer decides what measurements bear on it.

options.text: Because the mind is not physical, so no physical instrument can detect it.
options.why: The chapter argues the mind is physical. The limit is about the logic of the questions, not about the substance of minds.

options.text: Because the necessary measurements would be unethical to perform on people.
options.why: Ethics is not raised here. The obstacle is that measurement is the wrong kind of tool for this kind of question.

options.text: Because no instrument sensitive enough to count as a measurement of a mental state exists yet.
options.why: This would make the limit temporary, which is precisely what the chapter denies by locating it in the questions rather than the instruments.

items.stem: Most of the field has converged on one broad family of views. Why does the chapter say the disagreement is still live rather than closed?

options.text: Because a coherent position can almost always be resisted at some cost elsewhere.
options.why: Correct. Convergence here is the result of weighing consistency, fit and economy — not of a decisive result, so a determined opponent can hold out by giving something up in another place.

options.text: Because the converged position has never been stated precisely enough to test.
options.why: The chapter treats the third answer as clear and well-motivated. Its openness is not vagueness.

options.text: Because new evidence from neuroscience keeps reopening the question.
options.why: No such evidence is cited. The chapter says these questions are not settled by evidence in the first place.

options.text: Because the field is split roughly evenly, so no position has become the majority one.
options.why: It says the opposite: most contemporary brain and cognitive scientists have converged on one broad family.

items.stem: Where does the chapter's working definition of mind come from?

options.text: It is the information-processing picture the previous module introduced, adopted here as a working definition.
options.why: Correct. Module 0 gave the picture; §1.1.1 puts it to work as a definition so that the mind–body question can be asked precisely.

options.text: It is Descartes' definition, kept because it is the one the historical debate was conducted in.
options.why: Descartes appears as a defender of the first answer, not as the source of the book's definition, and the definition is deliberately neutral between the answers.

options.text: It is drawn from Marr's framework, which §1.2 sets out in full.
options.why: Marr's levels are a framework for explaining a system, not a definition of mind, and they are held back until §1.2.

options.text: It is a new definition written for this chapter, with no precedent earlier in the course.
options.why: It is explicitly a callback. Presenting it as new would lose the continuity the chapter is relying on.

items.stem: The chapter raises a motion sensor on a door and a smart thermostat immediately after giving its definition of mind. What work are those examples doing?

options.text: They satisfy the definition in miniature, and almost nobody wants to grant them minds.
options.why: Correct. The thermostat senses, compares against a goal, and acts — the very thing the definition names — and the discomfort that produces is the point rather than a flaw to be patched.

options.text: They are counterexamples that show the definition needs a further condition before it can be used.
options.why: The chapter adds no such condition. It offers the definition as a starting place rather than a test, and leaves where the line falls as a live debate.

options.text: They show that only systems with a biological substrate can satisfy the definition.
options.why: Both examples are artifacts and both satisfy it, which is the opposite of a biological requirement.

options.text: They illustrate that a system needs a goal state before it counts as processing information.
options.why: The thermostat has one and the motion sensor does not, yet both are offered. Goals are not the criterion being drawn.

items.stem: §1.1 says the famous positions are not boxes it sorted the world into, but labels for ways of answering a short sequence of questions. Set out that sequence in order, and show how at least three named positions fall out of it.
items.answer: First: do the physical facts fix the mental facts? Answer no and you get mind as a distinct kind of thing — substance dualism, and alongside it idealism and panpsychism. Answer yes and a second question follows: do our mental terms name anything real? Answer no and you get eliminative materialism, and behaviorism nearby. Answer yes and a third question follows: is a mental state identical to one specific physical state? Answer yes and you have identity theory, on which pain simply is the firing of C-fibers. Answer no and you arrive where most of the field sits, mind as a real property of the physical, which includes emergentism and functionalism. A fourth question is asked of that position rather than sorting it — how freely can such a mind be studied in its own terms — and it is a spectrum from strong autonomy to realization-sensitivity rather than a fork.
rubric: States the first question — whether the physical facts fix the mental facts — and the family that answering no produces.
States the question about whether mental terms refer, and names eliminative materialism as the no branch.
States the identity question, and names identity theory as the yes branch.
Names at least three positions and attaches each to the answer that produces it, rather than listing them independently.

items.stem: Class opened with misjudging a step on the stairs, told twice: vestibular system, startle reflex in about a tenth of a second, arms out, adrenaline — and then the stomach-drop, the jolt, the awful half-second. Why tell it twice?

options.text: Both descriptions are of the same instant, and how they relate is the problem the module addresses.
options.why: Correct. The physical telling leaves out no physical event, and the felt telling still seems to add something — so are they two accounts of one event, or one event in two languages?

options.text: To show that the physical description is incomplete until the felt one is added to it.
options.why: The lecture is careful that the physical description is complete in the sense of omitting no physical event. That is what makes the puzzle sharp rather than easy.

options.text: To show that the reflex happens before the feeling, so the feeling cannot have caused the reaction.
options.why: Timing was mentioned to convey how fast the reflex is, not to argue about causal order between the two descriptions.

options.text: To distinguish the parts of the episode that are conscious from the parts that are automatic.
options.why: That division is not what the pairing is for; both descriptions cover the whole instant rather than different portions of it.

pools.title: What Kind of Thing Is a Mind? The Three Answers

items.stem: What does functionalism claim a mental state is?

options.text: A state defined by the causal role it plays — by what brings it about and what it goes on to cause.
options.why: Correct. Functionalism defines a mental state by its position in a causal web, not by its material. Because a role can in principle be filled by different stuff, this is the view that most readily opens the door to machine minds.

options.text: A state defined by the particular biological material that happens to be carrying it out.
options.why: This is closer to identity theory, which ties a mental state to one specific physical state of the brain. Functionalism was formulated partly against that move, because it makes a state's material essential rather than incidental.

options.text: A state whose legitimacy rests on whether talking about it helps us predict behavior.
options.why: This describes instrumentalism, which is a claim about when mental vocabulary is warranted. Functionalism is a claim about what a mental state is, so the two answer different questions and can be held together.

options.text: A state that arises from organized matter the way wetness arises from many water molecules.
options.why: This is emergentism, a sibling view in the same family. Emergentism says that mental properties arise from organization; functionalism says more specifically what individuates them, namely causal role.

items.stem: Which view holds that our everyday vocabulary of beliefs and desires does not merely need refining, but picks out nothing real, so that a mature brain science will discard it?

options.text: Eliminative materialism
options.why: Correct. Eliminative materialism predicts that folk psychology will go the way of the four humours — not refined, but replaced by a description in terms of brains and behavior. (Class used phlogiston to make the same point; the chapter's case is the humours.)

options.text: Instrumentalism about mental states
options.why: Instrumentalism keeps the mental vocabulary and licenses it by its usefulness for prediction. It declines to say the vocabulary is true, which is a much weaker claim than saying it is empty.

options.text: Radical behaviorism
options.why: Behaviorism set inner states aside as unscientific to study, which is a restriction on method. Eliminative materialism makes the stronger claim that the states are not there to be found.

options.text: Identity theory
options.why: Identity theory keeps every mental term and identifies it with a physical state. Eliminativism denies there is anything for those terms to be identified with.

items.stem: What distinguishes emergentism from panpsychism?

options.text: Emergentism holds that mind appears only where matter is organized a certain way; panpsychism holds it is present in all matter.
options.why: Correct. The dividing question is whether organization is what brings mind about. Emergentism says yes, so a rock has none; panpsychism says experience is basic, so a rock has some faint degree of it.

options.text: Emergentism is a materialist position, whereas panpsychism is really a form of substance dualism dressed up in more contemporary vocabulary.
options.why: Both are attempts to stay within one kind of stuff, so neither is substance dualism. Panpsychism makes experience a basic feature of matter rather than a second substance alongside it.

options.text: Emergentism applies only to biological systems, whereas panpsychism covers artificial ones too.
options.why: Neither view is restricted by biology. Emergentism turns on how matter is organized, and organization is something an artificial system can have just as a brain can.

options.text: Emergentism denies that qualia exist at all, whereas panpsychism makes qualia fundamental.
options.why: Denying qualia is eliminativism's move, not emergentism's. Emergentism is comfortable saying that felt experience is real and that it arises from organization.

items.stem: An octopus behaves in every way we would expect of an animal in pain, but its nervous system contains nothing resembling the C-fibers of a human. A researcher concludes that the octopus therefore cannot be in pain. Which problem does that conclusion illustrate?

options.text: The chauvinism problem
options.why: Correct. Tying a mental state to one specific physical makeup means that anything built differently is ruled out by definition, no matter how it behaves. That is exactly the objection the chauvinism problem raises against identity theory.

options.text: The hard problem
options.why: The hard problem asks why any physical process is accompanied by felt experience at all. The researcher here is not puzzled about that; they are excluding a creature on the grounds of its hardware.

options.text: Explanatory separability
options.why: Explanatory separability is a question about method — how far the mind can be studied in its own terms. The researcher's error concerns what pain is, which is a question of ontology instead.

options.text: The just-so-story problem
options.why: Just-so stories are the risk run by evolutionary "why" claims asserted without evidence. No adaptive claim is being made here at all.

items.stem: Materialism and eliminative materialism are often run together, but a materialist need not be an eliminativist. Explain the difference, and say what further commitment eliminative materialism adds.
items.answer: Materialism is the commitment that the physical facts determine the mental facts — that mind is not a separate kind of stuff, free to vary independently of its physical nature. It is a shared starting point rather than a full position, and identity theory, eliminative materialism, and the "mind as a real property" family all begin from it. Eliminative materialism adds a claim about our vocabulary: that terms like belief and desire do not merely need refining but pick out nothing real, so a mature brain science will discard folk psychology rather than reduce it. A materialist can therefore reject eliminativism by holding that mental terms describe something genuine about organized physical systems.
rubric: Defines materialism as the claim that physical facts determine mental facts.
Notes that materialism is a starting point shared by several distinct positions.
Identifies eliminativism's extra commitment as a claim about the mental vocabulary, not about the stuff.
States the eliminativist prediction that folk psychology is discarded rather than reduced.

items.stem: A question about something's ontology is a question about what?

options.text: What kind of thing it is, and what its basic nature is.
options.why: Correct. "What kind of thing is a mind?" is an ontological question, which is why the chapter treats it as prior to questions about how the mind should be studied.

options.text: How it can be known, and what would count as evidence about it.
options.why: That is epistemology. The chapter keeps the two apart deliberately: what a mind is and how freely it can be studied are separate questions, asked in §1.1.2 and §1.1.5.

options.text: What it is for, and what problem it evolved to solve.
options.why: That is the computational question of §1.2, and for a biological trait an adaptive why. It asks about function rather than about basic nature.

options.text: What it is made of at the smallest scale that can still be measured.
options.why: Composition is one ontological question among others, but ontology is not restricted to the smallest scale, and the chapter's third answer is precisely that mind is a property rather than a constituent.

items.stem: In class we imagined two systems physically identical down to the last particle, in the same state at the same instant, and asked whether they must have exactly the same mind. What does answering "yes, they must" commit you to?

options.text: Materialism — the commitment that the physical facts fix the mental ones.
options.why: Correct. The test sorts the first answer from the other two and does no more than that. It narrows the field rather than settling it, and the argument left over is the interesting one.

options.text: Identity theory, since identical physical states would have to be identical mental states.
options.why: The test does not reach that far. Identity theory is one materialist option, and the answer "yes" is equally available to functionalists and emergentists who reject it.

options.text: The view that a machine could have a mind, since physical duplication is all that is required.
options.why: Nothing about machines follows yet. A materialist can still hold that only biological organization produces a mind, which the chapter notes is a live position.

options.text: Eliminative materialism, since there is nothing left for mental vocabulary to pick out.
options.why: Answering "yes" says the physical fixes the mental. It says nothing about whether our everyday mental words name anything real, which is a further question.

items.stem: What is multiple realizability?

options.text: That one and the same mental state can be realized in different physical systems and materials.
options.why: Correct. The chapter's parallel is temperature, which one arrangement of molecules does not monopolize, and it is the idea that ties the mind–brain question to the machine question.

options.text: That one physical brain state can give rise to several different mental states at once.
options.why: This reverses the relation. The claim is many physical realizations of one mental state, not many mental states from one physical state.

options.text: That a mental state can be described at several different levels of analysis.
options.why: That is the levels framework of §1.2. Multiple realizability is a claim about what can carry a mental state, not about how many ways it can be described.

options.text: That the same behavior can be produced by systems that are in quite different mental states.
options.why: This is a claim about behavior underdetermining mental states. Multiple realizability concerns the physical substrate of a state, not the behavior it produces.

items.stem: The chapter brings in temperature to mark two borders around its own answer. Which pair of claims about mind does the comparison help it establish?

options.text: That mind is identical to no one arrangement, and arises only where matter is organized suitably.
options.why: Correct. Countless arrangements count as the same temperature, and that parallel separates the third answer from identity theory. The second border is drawn by contrast rather than by parallel: a rock has a temperature but no mind, because it is not arranged to have one, which is what separates the third answer from panpsychism.

options.text: That a higher-level property is always reducible in principle, and that reduction never licenses elimination.
options.why: The chapter does argue that reduction need not eliminate, but temperature is used to draw borders with two named positions rather than to establish a general thesis about reduction.

options.text: That thermodynamics was replaced by statistical mechanics, and that psychology will likewise be replaced by neuroscience.
options.why: The chapter says the reverse on both counts. Thermodynamics still does real work, and that is precisely why the mental level is not expected to be discarded.

options.text: That felt experience is a basic feature of matter, and that organization determines only its degree.
options.why: This is panpsychism, which the temperature case is used to argue against. On the third answer a rock has no faint share of mind at all.

items.stem: The third answer accuses the dualist of a category error. What is the error?

options.text: Asking what kind of thing a mind is, when a mind is not a thing at all.
options.why: Correct. Mass is not an object tucked inside a rock; it is something the rock has. The third answer says mind is a property of that kind, so the dualist's question was malformed before any answer was given.

options.text: Assuming the mind is physical when the question of what it is made of has not been settled.
options.why: The charge runs the other way. The dualist is accused of accepting the question's framing too readily, not of prejudging the answer toward the physical.

options.text: Treating consciousness and the rest of mental life as though they were the same phenomenon.
options.why: The chapter does keep those apart, but that is a separate caution. The category error concerns thing versus property.

options.text: Inferring from our inability to imagine a physical mind that a physical mind is impossible.
options.why: This resembles a complaint about the zombie argument, which is a different objection. The category error is about what sort of item a mind is.

items.stem: Two researchers both hold that mind is a real property of the physical. One expects a machine could have a mind; the other doubts it. What question are they actually disagreeing about?

options.text: Whether a mind's physical basis has to be biological, which staying within the third answer leaves open.
options.why: Correct. The third answer is the home of "yes, in principle," but it does not settle substrate. Doubts concentrate on consciousness rather than on the cognitive capacities, and the doubt is a bet about substrate rather than a lapse into dualism.

options.text: Whether the physical facts fix the mental facts, which is the question that divides materialists from dualists.
options.why: They have already agreed on that. Both hold the third answer, which is a materialist position, so the physical-duplicate test would give them the same verdict.

options.text: Whether our everyday mental vocabulary picks out anything real.
options.why: That is the eliminativist's question, and the third answer answers it yes by definition. Both researchers are on the same side of it.

options.text: Whether a mental state is identical to one specific physical state.
options.why: Answering no to that is what puts them both in the third answer rather than in identity theory. It is settled before their disagreement begins.

items.stem: What does substance dualism hold?

options.text: Mind and body are two kinds of substance, interacting but not reducible to one another.
options.why: Correct. The interaction is what makes it dualism rather than a denial that the physical matters, and the irreducibility is what separates it from every materialist position.

options.text: The mind is a property that physical matter has when organized in a certain way.
options.why: That is the third answer, which is materialist. Dualism denies that arranging matter could ever be enough.

options.text: Mental and physical vocabulary describe the same events, and neither is more fundamental.
options.why: This is closer to a two-descriptions view within materialism. Dualism claims two kinds of stuff, not two ways of talking.

options.text: Only mental substance exists, and the physical world is an appearance within a mind.
options.why: That is idealism, which the chapter calls the odd cousin — it keeps only the mental rather than positing two substances.

items.stem: What is materialism, as the chapter uses the term?

options.text: The commitment that the physical facts fix the mental facts.
options.why: Correct, and it is deliberately broad. It is the shared starting point of identity theory, eliminative materialism, and the "real property" view, which then disagree about everything after it.

options.text: The view that only matter exists and mental states are therefore illusions.
options.why: That is closer to eliminativism, which is one materialist option among several. A materialist can hold that mental states are perfectly real.

options.text: The view that a mental state is identical to one particular brain state.
options.why: That is identity theory, a specific materialism. Materialism itself does not require any one-to-one identity.

options.text: The methodological rule that psychology should study only what can be observed.
options.why: That is radical behaviorism, a claim about method rather than about what fixes what.

items.stem: What is a philosophical zombie?

options.text: A being physically identical to a person and behaving identically, but with no inner experience at all.
options.why: Correct. The physical and behavioral identity is essential to the thought experiment — anything less would make the missing experience unsurprising.

options.text: A person whose behavior is normal but whose reports about their own experience are unreliable.
options.why: Unreliable reporting still leaves experience present. The zombie is defined by having none.

options.text: A hypothetical system that has experiences but cannot report or act on them.
options.why: This inverts the case. The zombie acts perfectly and experiences nothing.

options.text: A being physically different from a person that nonetheless behaves exactly like one.
options.why: Physical identity is the whole point. A differently built system that behaves alike raises multiple realizability instead.

items.stem: The zombie argument is often heard as the claim that zombies exist. What is the argument actually doing?

options.text: Arguing that if such a being is coherently imaginable, the physical facts leave experience open.
options.why: Correct. The work is done by conceivability, not by existence. Nobody claims to have met a zombie, and the argument would not be improved if they had.

options.text: Arguing that we cannot know whether other people have inner experience.
options.why: That is the problem of other minds. The zombie case is aimed at what the physical facts settle, not at what we can know about each other.

options.text: Arguing that behavior is a poor guide to mental states, so behaviorism fails.
options.why: Behaviorism is refuted in the chapter on other grounds — language, reasoning, memory, planning. The zombie targets materialism generally.

options.text: Arguing that a system without experience could not sustain human behavior for long.
options.why: The thought experiment stipulates that it does, perfectly and indefinitely. Denying that would dissolve the case rather than answer it.

items.stem: The chapter gives two problems that make substance dualism unattractive as a scientific view. What are they?

options.text: How a non-physical mind could move physical neurons, and that a mind leaving no physical trace is one no experiment can find.
options.why: Correct. The first is the interaction problem, whose every answer seems to smuggle the mind back into the physical; the second places the view outside science by its very nature rather than by any failed test.

options.text: That it cannot explain felt experience, and that it conflicts with what neuroscience has discovered.
options.why: Explaining felt experience is dualism's chief attraction — it sidesteps the puzzle by denying matter has to produce it.

options.text: That it is internally inconsistent, and that no serious philosopher has defended it.
options.why: The chapter does not call it inconsistent, and it credits Descartes and a long tradition before him with defending it.

options.text: That it cannot account for language and reasoning, and that it dominated psychology for forty years.
options.why: Both of those are said of radical behaviorism, which is a materialist position and the opposite kind of view.

items.stem: What does substance dualism imply about whether a machine could have a mind, and why?

options.text: Never — engineering only arranges physical parts, and a mind requires something non-physical.
options.why: Correct, and it is a flat answer rather than a cautious one. However fluent the machine, on this view it is an empty mechanism saying the right things with no one inside.

options.text: Possibly, if the machine were built from the right materials.
options.why: Materials are beside the point on this view. No arrangement of any physical stuff supplies the non-physical ingredient.

options.text: Yes in principle, since a mind is defined by what it does rather than what it is made of.
options.why: That is functionalism, which sits in the third answer and is the position most open to machine minds.

options.text: Faintly, in the way a stone has a mind — but no more for being a computer.
options.why: That is panpsychism, the family's lone exception on machines, and it reaches that verdict by a different route.

items.stem: The chapter is careful to state dualism's appeal before rejecting it. What does it credit the view with?

options.text: Sidestepping how matter could produce felt experience, by denying that matter has to.
options.why: Correct. It also honors the strong sense that consciousness is not merely more chemistry, and leaves room for a soul that outlasts the body. The problems are separate from the appeal, and the chapter grants both.

options.text: Fitting the findings of neuroscience more economically than its rivals.
options.why: Parsimony and fit with neuroscience are credited to the reductive family, which is the second answer.

options.text: Explaining how mental states can be shared across differently built systems.
options.why: That is multiple realizability, which belongs to the third answer and works against dualism.

options.text: Providing the clearest account of how the mind and brain interact.
options.why: Interaction is dualism's central difficulty, not its strength.

items.stem: What does identity theory claim about a mental state such as pain?

options.text: That it simply is a particular physical state of the brain — one event under two names.
options.why: Correct, and the strength of the claim matters. Not that the brain state causes the pain, and not that the two reliably co-occur, but that they are the same thing, on the model of heat turning out to be molecular motion.

options.text: That it is reliably caused by a particular brain state, which is why brain scans can detect it.
options.why: Causation is the weaker relation the theory explicitly rejects. Two events that cause one another are two events.

options.text: That it is whatever plays the pain role, in a brain or in anything else.
options.why: That is functionalism, which was formulated partly against identity theory precisely because roles can be filled by different stuff.

options.text: That talk of pain will eventually be dropped in favour of talk about neurons.
options.why: That is eliminativism. Identity theory keeps every mental term and identifies each with a physical state.

items.stem: In class, eliminative materialism's prediction about belief and desire was made concrete with a case from the history of chemistry. Which one, and what did it illustrate?

options.text: Phlogiston — once posited to explain burning, then dropped rather than refined.
options.why: Correct. The eliminativist's bet is that folk psychology goes the same way: not tidied up and matched to brain states, but replaced outright.

options.text: Alchemy's attempts to transmute lead into gold, which showed the goal itself was incoherent.
options.why: The point is not that a goal was incoherent but that a term turned out to name nothing. Alchemy was not the case used.

options.text: The discovery that heat is molecular motion, which showed an everyday concept surviving reduction.
options.why: That case appears in the lecture, but as the model for identity theory — the concept kept and identified with something lower down. It is the opposite fate.

options.text: The periodic table's prediction of undiscovered elements, which showed a framework being vindicated.
options.why: Vindication is not the eliminativist's prediction for folk psychology. The analogy has to be a concept that was discarded.

items.stem: What did radical behaviorism urge psychology to do?

options.text: Study only observable behavior, and set aside talk of inner mental states as unscientific.
options.why: Correct. Associated with Watson and Skinner, it dominated from roughly 1920 to 1960 before the cognitive revolution reopened the door to inner processes.

options.text: Study inner mental states, but only through their measurable physical correlates in the brain.
options.why: Behaviorism set inner states aside rather than seeking correlates for them; the brain was as unavailable to it as the mind.

options.text: Treat mental vocabulary as useful for prediction while declining to say it is true.
options.why: That is instrumentalism, a claim about when mental talk is warranted rather than a restriction on what may be studied.

options.text: Explain behavior by the beliefs and desires that produce it, stated precisely.
options.why: That is folk psychology made rigorous, which is close to what behaviorism was reacting against.

items.stem: What broke behaviorism's dominance?

options.text: It could not account for the things minds most obviously do — language, reasoning, remembering, planning.
options.why: Correct, and the failure was internal rather than philosophical. The cognitive revolution of the 1960s and 70s reopened the door to a science of inner processes precisely because these capacities needed one.

options.text: Brain imaging made inner mental states directly observable, removing the reason to exclude them.
options.why: Imaging came far later and is not the chapter's account. The break was about explanatory failure, not new instruments.

options.text: It was shown to be logically inconsistent with materialism.
options.why: Behaviorism is a materialist position; there was no such inconsistency to find.

options.text: Its predictions about animal learning were overturned by later experiments.
options.why: The chapter names higher capacities, not animal learning results, as what it could not handle.

items.stem: The chapter says a higher-level idea can meet one of three fates. What are they, and which does it say the mind fits?

options.text: Discarded as naming nothing, identified with something lower, or grounded without being replaced — the mind fits the third.
options.why: Correct. The four humours were discarded, heat was identified with molecular motion, and temperature is grounded in statistical mechanics while thermodynamics still does real work. Most of the field thinks mental vocabulary fits that last pattern.

options.text: Discarded, identified, or shown to be a useful fiction — and the mind fits the third.
options.why: A useful fiction is instrumentalism's option, and it is not one of the three fates the chapter lays out.

options.text: Confirmed, refined, or refuted by experiment — and the mind is still being refined.
options.why: This is a general picture of theory change rather than the chapter's three, and none of the three turns on experiment.

options.text: Discarded, identified, or grounded — and the mind fits the second, as identity theory holds.
options.why: The three fates are right, but the second is precisely the option the chapter argues against, on the strength of multiple realizability.

items.stem: The chapter calls the second answer "half right." Which half, and what is the error?

options.text: Right that the mind is physical and the brain carries explanatory weight; wrong to discard mental-level explanation.
options.why: Correct. The chapter grants the reductive family its materialism and its respect for neuroscience, and objects only to the further step, which is why the third answer is a correction rather than a rejection.

options.text: Right that mental vocabulary is useful; wrong that it corresponds to anything real.
options.why: This inverts eliminativism, which denies the correspondence rather than the usefulness, and it is not what the chapter credits.

options.text: Right about identity theory; wrong about eliminative materialism.
options.why: The chapter's verdict is not split between the two members. Both share the error, which is about explanation rather than about which reductive variant is correct.

options.text: Right that psychology works; wrong that its findings can be stated without neuroscience.
options.why: That psychology works is the third answer's argument, offered against the second.

items.stem: What reason does the chapter give for keeping psychological explanations rather than replacing them with neuron-by-neuron ones?

options.text: They work, and add what a neuron-level story does not.
options.why: Correct. The word doing the work is in practice: the calculation is hopeless, and higher-level accounts are how the science actually gets done. Most sciences reduce without eliminating, as thermodynamics and the gene both show.

options.text: The neuron-level facts are not yet known well enough to attempt the replacement.
options.why: This would make the case temporary. The chapter's point holds even granting complete neural knowledge.

options.text: Mental states are not physical, so a physical vocabulary cannot capture them.
options.why: The chapter is materialist. Mental states are physical; the argument is about levels of explanation, not about substance.

options.text: Psychological explanations are easier to teach, even if less accurate.
options.why: No trade of accuracy for convenience is claimed. They are said to add something a lower-level account lacks.

items.stem: Multiple realizability is said to do two jobs at once. What are they?

options.text: It defeats the chauvinism problem, and it turns "could a non-brain have a mind?" into a real scientific question.
options.why: Correct. No single physical state can be pain if pain turns up in systems with no such state — which frees the third answer from identity theory's chauvinism and, in the same move, makes the machine question empirical rather than confused.

options.text: It defeats the chauvinism problem, and it establishes that machines already have minds.
options.why: Nothing about actual machines follows. It makes the question askable, which is a much weaker and more useful claim.

options.text: It explains felt experience, and it shows why psychology cannot be reduced to neuroscience.
options.why: Felt experience is exactly what the third answer's critics say it leaves out, and irreducibility rests on a separate argument.

options.text: It refutes materialism, and it supports the view that mind is a distinct kind of thing.
options.why: It is offered within materialism, as the reason a materialist need not be an identity theorist.

items.stem: Statistical mechanics explains where the laws of thermodynamics come from. What does the chapter draw from the fact that nobody therefore abandoned temperature?

options.text: A concept can be grounded in a deeper theory and still do real work, so reduction need not mean replacement.
options.why: Correct. Thermodynamics still tells an engineer how an engine must behave, and countless molecular arrangements count as one temperature — which is why the case does double duty against identity theory too.

options.text: That deeper theories are usually wrong about the phenomena they claim to explain.
options.why: Statistical mechanics is not being questioned. The point concerns what survives a successful reduction.

options.text: That temperature is not a real property, only a convenient summary.
options.why: The chapter treats temperature as a genuine property matter has, and uses it as the model for mind being real.

options.text: That the two theories contradict each other and only one can be kept.
options.why: They are presented as fitting together, one grounding the other. No contradiction arises.

items.stem: The levels of analysis approach is named in §1.1.4 as a fourth member of the third answer, and then set aside. Why?

options.text: Because it is the framework the rest of the course runs on, so the whole of §1.2 is given to it.
options.why: Correct. It is introduced as one way of spelling out "mind is a real property of the physical," and then developed at length rather than in passing.

options.text: Because it is the weakest member of the family and is included only for completeness.
options.why: The chapter treats it as the framework worth building the course around, which is the opposite of a weak member.

options.text: Because it belongs to the second answer and appears here only by contrast.
options.why: It is explicitly placed within the third answer, alongside emergentism and functionalism.

options.text: Because it is a claim about method rather than about what the mind is.
options.why: That describes explanatory separability, the §1.1.5 question. The levels approach is offered as an account of what a mind is as well as how to study it.

items.stem: State the third answer to the mind–body problem, and explain how it differs from both of the other two rather than being a compromise between them.
items.answer: The third answer is that mind is a real property of physical stuff — a property a system has when its parts are organized and active in the right way, as real as the matter itself but not a separate ingredient added to it. It differs from the first answer by being materialist: no non-physical substance is posited, and the physical facts fix the mental ones. It differs from the second by holding that mental terms refer to something real and that mental-level explanation is not redundant. It is not a midpoint between them, because it rejects the question both of them were answering. The dualist asks what kind of thing a mind is and reaches for a special non-physical kind; the third answer says a mind is not a thing at all but a property, the way mass is something a rock has rather than an object inside it. That is a category error charge, not a compromise.
rubric: States the third answer: mind is a real property of suitably organized physical matter.
Distinguishes it from the first answer by its materialism — no separate substance.
Distinguishes it from the second by keeping mental terms as referring and mental explanation as doing real work.
Explains that it rejects the shared question rather than splitting the difference — the category error of asking what thing a mind is.

items.stem: Class opened with someone who has talked to a companion app daily for a year — it remembers, it asks how their week went, it says it missed them — and asked whether there is anything it is like to be that app. What was the uncomfortable follow-up?

options.text: Not how you would argue about it, but how you would settle it with someone who disagreed.
options.why: Correct. Most people have a firm intuition here, and the difficulty of converting that intuition into something that could persuade a dissenter is the whole subject of the day.

options.text: Whether someone designing the app intended it to produce that reaction in its users.
options.why: Designer intent bears on the computational "why" of an artifact, but it was not the question put to the room.

options.text: Whether the person's attachment to the app was itself evidence that the app has a mind.
options.why: The lecture treats the attachment as real and as beside the point; nothing was inferred from it about the app.

options.text: Whether the app would still behave that way if its memory were switched off.
options.why: No such manipulation was proposed. The question was epistemic — how the disagreement could be resolved at all.

items.stem: Class said of the chauvinism problem that "the name is doing real work." What did it mean?

options.text: The view has quietly made our physical make-up the standard for having a mental state.
options.why: Correct. Chauvinism is not a loose insult here: identity theory does not merely doubt that an octopus feels pain, it rules the question out by definition, on the grounds that its fibres are not ours. The lecture called this the pivot of the hour.

options.text: That the objection is rhetorical rather than substantive, so it can be set aside.
options.why: The lecture treats it as the strongest objection to the second answer and the reason most people leave it, which is the opposite of setting it aside.

options.text: That a distributed nervous system cannot support the kind of unified state pain would have to be.
options.why: No such conclusion is drawn. The octopus's distributed nervous system is offered as a difference from ours, never as a deficit.

options.text: That behavioural evidence becomes unreliable once an animal is anatomically unlike us.
options.why: The lecture treats the octopus's behaviour as genuinely suggestive — guarding an injured arm, avoiding where it was hurt — which is what gives the case its force.

items.stem: Which view holds that the mind just is the brain, so that a separate mental vocabulary earns its keep only as a convenient shorthand, if at all?

options.text: The second answer — mind as nothing but the physical
options.why: Correct. Behaviorism, identity theory and eliminative materialism are its members, and what unites them is the claim that mental talk adds nothing a physical vocabulary could not in principle replace.

options.text: The third answer — mind as a real property of the physical
options.why: This one insists mental terms refer to something real and that mental-level explanation does work no neuron-level story can do.

options.text: Substance dualism
options.why: Dualism holds that the mind is not physical at all, which is the opposite commitment.

options.text: Panpsychism
options.why: Panpsychism makes experience a basic feature of all matter, so it neither reduces the mind to the brain nor treats mental talk as shorthand.

items.stem: The chapter compares folk psychology to the four humours. What does the comparison claim will happen to beliefs and desires?

options.text: They will be dropped outright rather than refined, because there is nothing for the words to name.
options.why: Correct, and the contrast is with heat, which was kept and identified with molecular motion. The eliminativist's bet is on the other fate: replacement, not reduction.

options.text: They will be refined into more precise concepts once neuroscience matures.
options.why: Refinement is exactly what the analogy denies. The humours were not sharpened up; they were abandoned.

options.text: They will be shown to be identical to particular brain states, one for each.
options.why: That is identity theory's prediction, which keeps every mental term rather than eliminating it.

options.text: They will remain useful for everyday purposes while ceasing to be scientifically respectable.
options.why: That is closer to instrumentalism. Eliminativism makes the stronger claim that the states are not there at all.

pools.title: Studying the Mind, and Where the Field Sits

items.stem: What question does explanatory separability ask?

options.text: How far the mind can be studied in its own terms rather than through the brain.
options.why: Correct. It is a question about method, and the chapter is careful to mark it as distinct from the question of what the mind is made of.

options.text: Whether mental states can be separated from one another cleanly enough to be studied individually.
options.why: This concerns how mental life divides up. Explanatory separability concerns the relation between the mental level and the physical detail beneath it.

options.text: Whether the mind could continue to exist separately from the body that realizes it.
options.why: That is a dualist question about ontology, and the chapter raises separability only after the ontological question has been answered materialistically.

options.text: Whether psychology's findings can be replicated independently of the neuroscience that motivated them.
options.why: Replication is a question about evidence. Separability is about whether a mental-level theory can stand without the physical details in view.

items.stem: What separates the strong-autonomy pole from the cautious pole on explanatory separability?

options.text: Whether a theory can abstract away from how a mind is realized.
options.why: Correct. Strong autonomy says psychology stands to neuroscience roughly as chemistry stands to physics; the cautious pole holds that the details of realization shape what a mental state can be.

options.text: Whether the mind is physical at all, with strong autonomy allowing that it might not be.
options.why: Both poles sit inside the third answer and take the mind to be physical. The disagreement is about method, not about substance.

options.text: Whether psychology's concepts will eventually be replaced by neuroscientific ones.
options.why: That is eliminativism's prediction, and neither pole holds it. Even the cautious pole keeps the mental level and only denies it can float free.

options.text: Whether psychology should describe mental states in everyday vocabulary or in technical terms.
options.why: Choice of vocabulary is not what divides the poles. Both are willing to use technical mental-level terms; they differ over whether such a theory can stand without the physical detail.

items.stem: A researcher says: "I have shown the mind is a real property of organized physical matter, so psychology can proceed without waiting on neuroscience." What has been assumed without argument?

options.text: That settling what a mind is also settles how freely it can be studied in its own terms.
options.why: Correct. The chapter separates these deliberately. The ontological answer leaves the methodological question open, and the field is genuinely split on it.

options.text: That the mind is physical, which the argument was supposed to establish rather than assume.
options.why: The researcher does argue for this, and the chapter agrees with the conclusion. The unearned step is the one that follows it.

options.text: That psychology and neuroscience study the same object, which is what would need showing.
options.why: Both poles grant that they study the same object. The disagreement is over how much of it can be described without the other's vocabulary.

options.text: That a real property must be one that experiments can detect.
options.why: The chapter treats the third answer as the scientifically tractable one, so this is not an assumption that gets the researcher into trouble here.

items.stem: Why does the chapter build the named positions out of a sequence of questions rather than presenting them as a list of schools?

options.text: Because the positions are labels for ways of answering the questions.
options.why: Correct. Presented as a roster, the positions look like arbitrary rival camps; arrived at through the questions, each one is visibly the consequence of a particular answer.

options.text: Because a list would have to be exhaustive, and there are too many named positions to cover.
options.why: Length is not the objection. The chapter does present eight positions in a table; what it declines to do is start from them.

options.text: Because the named positions are historical curiosities that no current researcher holds.
options.why: The chapter says the opposite: most of the field holds a position in the third family, and the disagreement remains live.

options.text: Because the questions can be settled experimentally while the positions cannot.
options.why: None of the questions in this section are settled experimentally, which the chapter states plainly at the outset.

items.stem: Why does the chapter say the disagreement about explanatory separability has consequences, rather than being a merely verbal dispute? Say what turns on it.
items.answer: What turns on it is how far a science of the mind can float free of a science of the brain. On the strong-autonomy view psychology can build and test theories in its own vocabulary and treat the implementation as someone else's problem, so a theory that never mentions neurons can still be complete. On the cautious view a theory that abstracts away from body and brain will miss something, possibly something critical, because how a mind is realized shapes what it can be; two systems that look alike from a distance may not share a mental state unless they are organized alike underneath. The practical difference is whether neuroscientific detail is a constraint psychology must answer to or a level it may safely ignore.
rubric: States that what is at stake is how independent a science of the mind can be from a science of the brain.
Describes the strong-autonomy consequence: theories in mental vocabulary can stand on their own.
Describes the cautious consequence: abstracting away from realization risks missing something that matters.
Notes that the levels are separable but not independent — each can be asked about alone, yet the answers constrain one another.

items.stem: Summing up §1.1, where does the chapter say contemporary brain and cognitive science sits?

options.text: The mind is a real property of the physical, dependent on it yet explained in its own terms.
options.why: Correct, and the last clause is the honest part: the ontological question has an answer most of the field accepts, while the methodological one in §1.1.5 remains genuinely open.

options.text: The mind is a real property of the physical, and psychology can therefore proceed independently of neuroscience.
options.why: That is the strong-autonomy pole specifically, and the chapter presents the field as split on it rather than settled there.

options.text: The mind is identical to brain states, and mental vocabulary survives only as shorthand.
options.why: That is the second answer, which the chapter argues is half right and stops short of endorsing.

options.text: The field has not converged, and the three answers remain equally well supported.
options.why: The chapter reports convergence on the third answer, while noting that a coherent rival can still be defended at a cost.

items.stem: §1.1.6 maps the three answers onto the named positions. Which grouping is the chapter's?

options.text: A distinct kind of thing: dualism, idealism. Nothing but the physical: behaviorism, identity theory, eliminativism. A real property: emergentism, functionalism.
options.why: Correct, and seeing the grouping is more useful than memorising the roster — each position is just a label for a way of answering the sequence of questions.

options.text: A distinct kind of thing: dualism, panpsychism, emergentism. Nothing but the physical: behaviorism, identity theory. A real property: functionalism, eliminativism.
options.why: Two are misplaced. Emergentism holds that mind arises from organised matter, which is the third answer; eliminativism denies mental terms refer at all, which is the second.

options.text: A distinct kind of thing: dualism. Nothing but the physical: everything else, differing only in emphasis.
options.why: This collapses the distinction the whole section is built to draw, between denying mental vocabulary and grounding it.

options.text: A distinct kind of thing: dualism, idealism. Nothing but the physical: emergentism, functionalism. A real property: identity theory.
options.why: The last two groups are swapped. Identity theory equates a mental state with one physical state, which is the reductive answer.

items.stem: §1.1 ends by saying that "study the mind at its own level" is not yet a working claim. What is missing, and where is it supplied?

options.text: Nothing has been said about what the levels are, or how they relate to the brain beneath.
options.why: Correct. The phrase has a satisfying ring and no content until the levels are named and their relations spelled out, which is exactly the job §1.2 takes on.

options.text: The claim lacks experimental support, which §1.2 provides through the vision case.
options.why: Vision is used as a demonstration of the framework, not as evidence that a mental level exists. The gap is conceptual rather than evidential.

options.text: It has not been shown that most researchers accept it, which §1.2.3 establishes.
options.why: §1.2.3 shows the levels line up with existing disciplines, which is a different point from counting adherents.

options.text: The mind has not yet been shown to be physical, which §1.2 assumes rather than argues.
options.why: §1.1 already settled that. What is outstanding is what "its own level" means.

items.stem: Having laid out the two poles on explanatory separability, what does the chapter do next?

options.text: Declines to settle between them, and moves to a framework for laying the levels side by side.
options.why: Correct. Neither pole is obviously right, and the disagreement decides how far a science of mind can float free of a science of the brain — which is why §1.2 supplies Marr's levels rather than a verdict.

options.text: Argues for the strong-autonomy pole, since psychology is a science in its own right.
options.why: That pole is presented as one wing of the third answer, not as the chapter's conclusion.

options.text: Argues for the cautious pole, on the strength of embodied cognition.
options.why: Embodied cognition is named as pulling that way, but it is offered as one consideration rather than a decisive one.

options.text: Concludes that the question is unanswerable and sets it aside permanently.
options.why: The chapter treats it as live and consequential, and returns to it in §1.2.5 with the constraints between levels.

pools.title: One System, Many Kinds of Explanation

items.stem: In class we asked three questions about a leaf — what it is for, by what strategy, and what it is made of — and then asked which of the three is the real explanation. What was the answer?

options.text: The question is malformed: each answers something the others leave untouched.
options.why: Correct. The chemistry does not make it false that the leaf captures light, and knowing what it is for does not tell you it uses chloroplasts. The example was chosen because there is nothing it is like to be a leaf, so nothing about minds can cloud the point.

options.text: The chemical one, because the other two are shorthand that a complete chemistry would let us drop.
options.why: This is exactly the reflex the example was built to defeat, and the chapter resists it for the same reasons it refused to throw out the mind in favor of the brain.

options.text: The one about what it is for, because Marr held that the computational level comes first.
options.why: Marr's ordering claim is about where analysis should start, and the chapter flags it as contested. It is not a claim that one answer is the real one.

options.text: It depends on the discipline asking, since each field's answer is real within its own frame.
options.why: The chapter's claim is stronger and less relativist than this. All three answers are real facts about the leaf, not descriptions valid only relative to a viewpoint.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what would a complete wiring diagram of the brain still fail to tell you?

options.text: What problem a given circuit solves, and by what series of steps it solves it.
options.why: Correct. Those are further, real facts about the system, and no amount of detail about the tissue hands them to you — which is the same point the heart makes one level down.

options.text: Which neurons connect to which, since connectivity has to be inferred from activity rather than read off.
options.why: A wiring diagram is precisely a record of which neurons connect to which. This describes a limit the diagram does not have.

options.text: Whether the mind is a real property of the physical or merely a convenient shorthand.
options.why: §1.1 settles this by argument rather than by wiring, and the chapter does not present the diagram's limits as bearing on it.

options.text: Which parts of the brain are densely interconnected and which are relatively isolated.
options.why: A complete wiring diagram answers this directly, since it is a fact about connections. The gaps the chapter names lie at the other two levels.

items.stem: A student argues that talk of "problems" and "strategies" is loose shorthand that will be dropped once the tissue is fully understood. The chapter says this reflex has already been answered. Where?

options.text: In §1.1, where the mind was not thrown out in favor of the brain.
options.why: Correct. The chapter treats the move as the same error in a new place: a higher-level account that does real work is not made redundant by a complete lower-level one.

options.text: In §1.1, where the interaction problem showed that non-physical explanations cannot be scientific.
options.why: The interaction problem is an objection to dualism. It gives no reason to keep or discard a higher level of physical explanation.

options.text: In §1.2.2, where Marr argued that analysis should run from the top down.
options.why: Marr's ordering claim is about method and the chapter marks it as contested, so it would be a weak place to rest the argument.

options.text: Nowhere yet — the chapter grants the point here and answers it only in §1.2.5.
options.why: §1.2.5 adds the constraints between levels, but the reflex is met here and the answer is credited to §1.1.

items.stem: Pick any everyday artifact or organ other than the heart or a leaf. State the three questions the chapter asks about one object, answer all three for your example, and say why the three answers do not compete.
items.answer: Take a bicycle brake. What problem is being solved: bringing a moving rider to a controlled stop without throwing them over the handlebars. By what strategy: convert a small hand force into a large clamping force applied to the wheel rim, so that friction converts the bicycle's motion into heat. In what physical stuff: a lever, a steel cable in a housing, and rubber pads squeezing an aluminium rim. The three do not compete because each answers a question the others leave untouched — the description of cable and pads does not say what the assembly is for, and knowing it is for stopping does not tell you the strategy is friction rather than, say, a motor running in reverse. A full understanding needs all three.
rubric: Names the three questions: what problem is solved, by what strategy, and in what physical stuff.
Gives a specific answer at each of the three levels for one chosen example.
States that the answers do not compete, because each addresses a question the others leave open.
Shows that fixing one level does not fix another — the physical account does not yield the purpose, or the purpose the strategy.

items.stem: The chapter says the heart's strategy — pushing fluid one way through a system of one-way valves — can be described without naming a single protein. Why does that matter?

options.text: It shows the strategy is a fact about the solution, not about the tissue that happens to run it.
options.why: Correct — you could state that strategy without even knowing whether the pump was built from biological tissue or metal, which is exactly what makes it a separate level of description from the muscle fibres and valves that implement it.

options.text: It shows the strategy is easier to discover than the physical details, so it should be studied first.
options.why: Ease of discovery is not the point, and the chapter treats top-down ordering as a contested claim rather than an established one.

options.text: It shows the proteins are irrelevant to how the heart actually performs its job.
options.why: They are entirely relevant at their own level. The claim is that the strategy can be stated without them, not that they do not matter.

options.text: It shows that any pump built on the same principle would count as a heart.
options.why: Nothing about what counts as a heart follows. The point concerns what a description at this level does and does not have to mention.

items.stem: Class introduced the framework through Marr's line that studying vision by studying neurons is like studying a bird's flight by studying only feathers. What was the complaint?

options.text: "How does a bird fly" is a question about airfoils and lift, which no amount of feather detail answers.
options.why: Correct, and the lecture was careful that this is not anti-neuroscience: feathers are not irrelevant to flight, you cannot fly without them. The mismatch is between the question and the level it is asked at.

options.text: Feathers are a minor component of flight, so they were a poorly chosen thing to study in the first place.
options.why: The lecture explicitly denies this. The problem is not that the parts are unimportant but that the question being asked is not about them.

options.text: The neuroscience of the 1970s used methods too crude to reveal what visual neurons were really doing.
options.why: The lecture says the opposite — the field was learning an enormous amount about individual neurons, and that was exactly the puzzle.

options.text: Vision cannot be understood at the implementational level, so that level should be set aside.
options.why: Marr's conclusion is that all three levels are needed, not that any one of them should be abandoned.

items.stem: Why does the course adopt Marr's three levels rather than Aristotle's four questions or Dennett's three stances?

options.text: Not because they are uniquely correct, but because they line up with how the field already divides.
options.why: Correct, and the chapter is unusually candid about it. The frameworks overlap and mostly agree, so the choice rests on fit with the course's structure rather than on one being right.

options.text: Because Marr's framework was the only one developed specifically for information-processing systems.
options.why: Dennett's stances and the mechanistic tradition in philosophy of biology apply to such systems too; the chapter presents them as genuine alternatives.

options.text: Because Aristotle's and Dennett's versions have since been shown to be mistaken about explanation.
options.why: The chapter says they overlap and mostly agree with Marr's carving, not that they are wrong.

options.text: Because Marr's is the only carving that makes room for an evolutionary question about function.
options.why: The evolutionary reading of the computational level is supplied in §1.2.3; it is not what distinguishes Marr's version from the others.

pools.title: Marr’s Three Levels: Defined and Applied

items.stem: In Marr's framework, what question does the algorithmic level ask?

options.text: How the system solves its problem — by what procedure, and over what representations.
options.why: Correct. The algorithmic level is where cognitive psychology and much of artificial intelligence do their work, because both are in the business of specifying procedures and the representations they run on.

options.text: What physical machinery carries the process out, whether neurons, silicon, or gears.
options.why: That is the implementational level, the home ground of neuroscience. Marr's point is that one algorithm can run on very different machinery.

options.text: What problem the system is solving, and why solving it is worth anything at all.
options.why: That is the computational level. It comes first in Marr's ordering, and it is the level the course's evolutionary framing attaches to.

options.text: Whether the mind can be studied in its own terms rather than through the brain.
options.why: This is the question of explanatory separability, which runs across all three levels rather than sitting at any one of them.

items.stem: Which term names the evolutionary answer to the computational level's "why" question — the problem an organism's ancestors faced, such that solving it aided survival and reproduction?

options.text: The adaptive why
options.why: Correct. It is one of three sources of a computational goal, alongside a designer's intent for an artifact and a cultural practice for a learned skill, and it is what welds Marr's framework to the course's evolutionary organization.

options.text: Multiple realizability
options.why: Multiple realizability is about one state being realized in different materials. It is a claim about implementation rather than an answer to a "why" question.

options.text: The inverse problem
options.why: The inverse problem is the specific computational problem vision solves: recovering a three-dimensional scene from an image that underdetermines it. It is an instance, not the general notion.

options.text: Folk psychology
options.why: Folk psychology is the everyday framework of beliefs and desires we use to predict behavior. It plays no part in specifying a computational goal.

items.stem: A researcher describes vision as the problem of recovering a three-dimensional scene from a two-dimensional image that underdetermines it. At which of Marr's levels is that description pitched?

options.text: The computational level, because it states the problem being solved rather than the procedure or the hardware.
options.why: Correct. Naming vision as an inverse problem says what the system must achieve and why that is hard. No procedure has been specified, and no machinery has been mentioned.

options.text: The algorithmic level, because recovering a scene must be a step-by-step process running over some set of internal representations.
